blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the `root` of a binary tree, return `true` if it is a **valid binary search tree**: every node's left subtree holds only values **less** than the node, its right subtree only values **greater**, and both subtrees are BSTs too.

blocks.alt: The tree 5, 1, 6, null, null, 3, 7. Every parent and child pair looks fine, but 3 is in the right subtree of 5 while being smaller than 5, so the tree is not a BST. Passing down the allowed range catches it: 6's left child must lie between 5 and 6, and 3 doesn't.

elements.text: each node must fit the range its ancestors allow
elements.originalText: each node must fit the range its ancestors allow

blocks.code:
root = [2, 1, 3]                     ->  true
root = [5, 1, 4, null, null, 3, 6]   ->  false   (4 is in 5's right subtree)
root = [5, 1, 6, null, null, 3, 7]   ->  false   (3 is in 5's right subtree)
root = [2, 2, 2]                     ->  false   (no duplicates: strictly less / greater)

blocks.text: Checking only `left.val < node.val < right.val` at each node passes the tree above — and it's wrong. The rule is about **whole subtrees**. Two correct ways to enforce it: pass down the **range** each node must fit in, or check that the **in-order** walk is strictly increasing.
1. Brute force: compare with every value below
At each node, check that the largest value in its left subtree is smaller and the smallest value in its right subtree is bigger — then check both subtrees the same way.
**Time O(n²)** in the worst case (every node scans its whole subtree), **space O(h).**
The root may be anything. Going **left** narrows the range from above (everything there must be below this node); going **right** narrows it from below. Each node just checks that it fits its range.

blocks.caption: Each node carries the range its ancestors allow; one value outside it fails the tree.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(h).** Java and C++ use 64-bit bounds because a node may hold `Integer.MIN_VALUE` or `MAX_VALUE` itself.
A binary tree is a BST exactly when its in-order walk is **strictly increasing**. Walk it and compare each value with the previous one.
**Time O(n), space O(h).** It stops at the first value out of order.

blocks.alt: Compare with every value below: O(n²) time, O(h) space. Pass down the range: O(n) time, O(h) space. In-order increasing: O(n) time, O(h) space.

items: **Duplicates** — `[2, 2, 2]` is not a BST under the strict rule.
**Extreme values** — `[2147483647]` must be valid: don't use int bounds as "no limit".
**A grandchild out of range** — the trap above: `[5, 1, 6, null, null, 3, 7]`.
**Recover Binary Search Tree** — exactly two values were swapped: find them with the same in-order check (Pattern 3).
**Largest BST subtree / Maximum Sum BST** — validate every subtree bottom-up in one pass (Pattern 5).
**Validate with duplicates allowed on one side** — make one comparison non-strict.
